transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello. Thank you for seeing me. I suppose what brings me in is that, for the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always puttering around the house. Fixing things, arranging things, volunteering for just one more thing... even at 87, I have such a hard time just sitting down and being still. 

It's funny, actually, because just last week my daughter told me to sit and watch a movie with her, but I noticed the living room bookshelf was dusty. And you know, once you start dusting one shelf, you really have to do them all or it just looks uneven. While I was doing that, I actually found an old photo album tucked in the back from when my late husband and I took a trip to Florida in 1982. The humidity down there was just awful for my hair, I tell you, I looked like an absolute poodle the entire trip! We stayed at this little motel that had these bright pink flamingos painted on all the doors, and the ice machine kept making this terrible clanking noise all night... 

Oh, but anyway, what was I saying? Yes, I just can't seem to stop moving around and doing things, and I suppose it's getting a bit tiring.
Do you find that you worry a lot, even when there isn’t much going on, or do you feel restless or on edge much of the time?

Well, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier, really. I don't sit around fretting about things. But restless? Oh my, yes. It’s exactly like that. 

Like, when I’m at the senior center for our morning meetings, or sitting through those terribly long church announcements on Sundays, I get this awful ants-in-my-chair feeling. I just can't bear to sit there. I have to keep shifting around, or I'll stand up to get myself a cup of coffee, or I'll just sit there and straighten the papers and the church bulletins just to get through the hour. 

And you know, speaking of the bulletins, Brenda has been typing those up for our parish for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. Bless her heart, but her eyesight is just not what it used to be. Last week she accidentally printed that the choir practice was at 3:00 AM instead of PM! Can you imagine? Mildred actually called the pastor's house at midnight to ask if she needed to bring a flashlight to get up the church steps. Mildred is such a character... she used to make these wonderful peach cobblers for the summer bake sale, but then she decided peaches were getting too expensive at the grocery store, so she switched to rhubarb. I just can't stand rhubarb, it's so awfully stringy if you don't cook it down right, and she never puts enough sugar in it...
Have you ever had periods where you felt unusually energetic or excited, like you didn’t need as much sleep or that your thoughts were racing faster than usual?

Oh, heavens no. I wouldn't say I get unusually excited or anything like that, and I certainly need my sleep! If I don't get my seven hours, I'm just no good the next day. I usually try to be in bed by ten o'clock, right after the evening news. 

Although, speaking of sleep, I had the most terrible time getting to sleep last Thursday. The Johnsons next door got a new dog—a little terrier mix, I believe—and it was just yapping at the wind all night! They adopted him from that shelter over in Springfield. You know, Springfield is where my niece Sarah lives. She just had her third baby, a little boy named Oliver. I told her Oliver is a lovely name, but it always makes me think of Oliver Twist, asking for more gruel. Do you remember that old movie? The musical one? We took my daughter to see it in the theater when she was just a little thing, and she sang "Food, Glorious Food" at the dinner table for three weeks straight. Drove my poor husband absolutely up the wall, he finally had to bribe her with a new jump rope just to have a quiet supper... 

But no, what were we talking about? Oh, right, sleep and racing thoughts. No, nothing like that. Just my usual puttering around.
Do you ever feel down or lose interest in things you used to enjoy, like hobbies or spending time with family?

Goodness, no, I wouldn't say I feel down. I still enjoy my days very much. I love my gardening, even if my knees aren't quite what they used to be. I still go out every morning to check on my hydrangeas. 

Oh, and you know, the most peculiar thing happened with my hydrangeas this year. They were always a lovely shade of blue—I used to put coffee grounds in the soil, you know, my grandmother taught me that trick to keep the soil acidic. But this spring, they bloomed completely pink! I was so surprised. I asked Mr. Henderson down at the garden center about it, and he said it has something to do with the aluminum in the soil changing over time. Mr. Henderson is such a nice man, his grandson just started college up at the state university. He's studying architecture, I believe. Or maybe it was engineering? Something with bridges, I think. I always thought building bridges would be such a fascinating job, connecting places together. We drove over that new suspension bridge they built a few counties over when we went to visit my sister last Thanksgiving, and it was just marvelously tall. My sister made a wonderful turkey, but she always uses that canned cranberry sauce, the kind that comes out looking exactly like the can with the ridges still on it. I just can't abide it, I always make mine from scratch with a little orange zest...

But, oh dear, I'm rambling again, aren't I? What was the question? Something about feeling down? No, no, I don't feel down at all. I still enjoy everything I do, I just can't seem to sit still while I'm doing it!
Do you ever feel like you can't relax, even when you want to, or like you're always 'on' and can't slow down your body?

Well, yes, I suppose that’s exactly it. That’s really what brings me in today, if I’m being honest. For the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always puttering around, fixing this, arranging that, or volunteering for just one more thing. Even at 87 years old, I have the hardest time just sitting down and being still! 

Like yesterday, I sat down to read the Sunday paper, and before I knew it, I was up reorganizing the pantry shelves because the soup cans weren't facing forward. And speaking of soup, I found three cans of clam chowder that expired in 2019! Can you believe it? I usually buy the chicken noodle, the kind with the little star-shaped pasta. My grandson Tommy used to love those when he was little. He’s all grown up now, of course, just got a job at a bank downtown. He wears these very sharp suits, though I told him the blue one washes him out a bit. He has his mother’s complexion, you see, very fair. She burns if she even looks at the sun, poor dear. We took a trip to Florida back in '98, and she had to wear a big floppy hat the whole time... 

But yes, I just can't seem to relax. My body always feels like it has to be doing something.
Do you ever feel like you have to move or do something specific, like arranging things just so, in order to feel a sense of relief or to prevent something bad from happening?

Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I don't think anything bad is going to happen if my soup cans aren't facing forward, and I don't get any sort of... deep relief from it. It's not a worry thing at all. I just do it because I'm already up and my hands just need to be busy! 

Though, speaking of arranging things, I was dusting my china cabinet the other day, just keeping busy, you know. I have this beautiful set of Royal Doulton teacups that my late husband Arthur bought for our twenty-fifth anniversary. We took a lovely trip to London that year. Oh, London was marvelous, though the weather was frightfully dreary. It rained almost every single afternoon! We had to buy these enormous umbrellas from a little shop near Piccadilly Circus. The man who ran the shop had the thickest accent, I could barely understand a word he was saying, but he was so incredibly polite. He told us the best place to get fish and chips, wrapped right up in actual newspaper, you know. They don't do that anymore, I suppose, what with health codes and all that nonsense nowadays. 

My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she's on the neighborhood watch committee, and she's always talking about codes and regulations. She actually tried to tell me last month that my stone birdbath was too close to the property line! Can you imagine? I told her the robins certainly don't care about property lines, and they need a place to splash around just as much as anyone. She got all huffy and marched right back inside her house. She has that house painted a very loud shade of yellow, like a school bus...

But dear me, what were we talking about? Oh, right, doing things to stop bad things from happening. No, no, I don't have anything like that. Just busy hands, I suppose!
Do you ever notice that your restlessness or need to move is accompanied by physical symptoms like muscle tension, fatigue, or trouble concentrating?

Well, no, I wouldn't say I get tired or tense. I actually have quite a bit of energy for my age! My muscles feel just fine, though my joints, well, that's just getting older, isn't it? I still walk down to the end of the driveway every single afternoon to get the mail. 

Our mail carrier, Gary, he's such a sweetheart. He always makes sure to put rubber bands around the magazines so they don't blow away. It gets terribly windy on our street, especially in November. Last year, the wind was so strong it blew Mrs. Gable's patio umbrella straight into my rhododendrons! Oh, she was in such a tizzy about it. She came over in her housecoat to fetch it, and it was the most atrocious shade of mauve. I don't know who told her mauve was her color, but it certainly washes her out. I always say, if you have a winter complexion, you should stick to jewel tones. I had this gorgeous emerald green dress I wore to my niece's wedding back in... oh, it must have been 1985. They had a lovely reception at the country club, though the chicken was terribly dry. They served it with those little baby carrots, the ones that are perfectly uniform, which always makes me wonder how they grow them like that... 

But dear me, I've lost the thread again, haven't I? I'm so sorry. Did you ask about my muscles? No, no tension or fatigue or anything like that. Just the busy hands and the puttering!
Do you ever feel distressed or find that this restlessness gets in the way of enjoying your day or doing things you want to do?

Well, it does get in the way a bit, yes. I suppose it can be distressing. Like at the senior center, I've actually had to apologize after our committee meetings because I just can't sit still through them. And one of my friends there, she even suggested I take a smaller role at the sign-up table because my whole manner was apparently making things tense for everyone else. 

Which was a bit of a shock to hear, I must admit! I've been doing the sign-up table for the annual bake sale for five years now. We always have it in the spring, right around Easter. The pastel colors are just so cheerful after a long winter, don't you think? I usually bake my famous lemon pound cake. The secret is to use real lemon zest, not that artificial extract nonsense you get in the little bottles. My mother taught me that. She was a wonderful baker, though she made a terrible mess of the kitchen. Flour everywhere! My father would just shake his head and go out to the garage to tinker with his Oldsmobile. It was a 1957 Oldsmobile 88, a beautiful two-tone blue and white. They don't make cars like that anymore, all heavy steel and chrome. Now they're just little plastic bubbles, and you can't even tell them apart in the grocery store parking lot. I spent twenty minutes last Tuesday trying to unlock a silver Honda that wasn't even mine! The gentleman who owned it was very understanding, though he did look a bit startled...

But oh, dear, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Yes, it does bother me that I can't just sit and enjoy things anymore without feeling like I'm causing a fuss.
Have you ever had a period lasting several days or more where you felt unusually excited or energized, had racing thoughts, or found yourself doing or saying things much more quickly than usual?

Oh, no, nothing like that. I've never had any days where my thoughts were racing or I felt overly excited like that. Just my normal self, you know, just puttering around. 

Speaking of puttering, I was just doing that yesterday afternoon in the garden. I have a lovely patch of hydrangeas right by the back fence. You know, the trick to getting them to turn that beautiful deep blue is to put coffee grounds in the soil. It makes it more acidic, I believe. My husband Arthur, bless his heart, he used to drink the most awful, strong coffee. He'd brew it in this old percolator that sounded like a freight train in the mornings. I always preferred tea, myself. Earl Grey, usually, with just a splash of milk. We used to go to this little tea shop downtown, right on Main Street. It had the most charming lace curtains in the windows. It's a bank now, I think. Or maybe a real estate office? Everything downtown has changed so much. It's a shame, really. All the nice little shops are gone, replaced by these big, soulless buildings with glass fronts. 

My friend Beatrice, she lives down in Florida now, she says it's exactly the same down there. Strip malls as far as the eye can see! She moved down there after her husband passed. She bought a little condo in one of those communities with a golf course. I don't know why, she doesn't even play golf! She says she likes watching the little carts go by...

But oh, my goodness, listen to me rattle on! What was the question again? Racing thoughts? No, no, my thoughts don't race, they just... wander a bit, I suppose!
Would you say that this restlessness you feel is more about a need to be doing something, or is it more about feeling anxious or keyed up inside?

Well, it's definitely just a need to be doing something. I don't feel anxious or, you know, keyed up inside at all. I just like to keep my hands busy! 

Like knitting, for example. I've been knitting a lot more lately. I'm making a blanket for my grandnephew, little Tommy. He's just turning three next month, and he loves anything with trains on it. So I found this darling pattern with little steam engines all along the border. It's quite intricate, actually. You have to switch colors every few stitches, which means carrying the yarn across the back. If you pull it too tight, the whole thing puckers, and if it's too loose, little fingers can get caught in the loops. I learned that the hard way when I made a sweater for my own son, David, back in... oh, 1962, I think. He got his thumb stuck in a loose thread and pulled the whole sleeve unraveled right in the middle of Sunday school! The teacher, Mrs. Higgins, had to use a safety pin to hold it together until church let out. 

Mrs. Higgins was a lovely woman, though she wore the most overpowering perfume. Lily of the valley, I think it was. It would linger in the classroom for hours after she left. I always preferred a lighter scent, like rosewater. I used to buy it from the apothecary on the corner of Elm and Maple. They had those beautiful glass bottles with the little atomizers that you squeeze...

Oh, dear, there I go again! I am so sorry, doctor. But yes, to answer your question, no anxiety or feeling keyed up. Just the urge to be doing things!
Do you ever feel like something bad is going to happen or find yourself worrying about things even when there’s no clear reason to be concerned?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I don't sit around worrying about bad things happening out of the blue. I've always been more of an optimist, really. 

My sister, Eleanor, now she was the worrier in the family. She would fret over every little thing! I remember back when we were girls, we took a train trip down to Chicago with our parents. Oh, it must have been 1948, maybe '49. Eleanor was absolutely convinced we were going to leave our luggage on the platform. She checked the tags on those suitcases at least ten times before we even boarded. They were those beautiful hard-sided Samsonite cases, a lovely dark forest green. My mother had tied a little piece of yellow ribbon to the handles of ours so we could spot them easily. 

We stayed at the Palmer House, which was just magnificent back then. The lobby ceiling had these incredible painted frescoes. We had high tea in the Empire Room, and they served these tiny little cucumber sandwiches with the crusts cut off. I always thought that was such a waste of good bread! My mother used to save our bread crusts and make bread pudding out of them on Sundays. With raisins and a nice vanilla sauce... she'd bake it in this heavy ceramic dish that had little blue flowers painted around the rim. I wonder whatever happened to that dish? I think my niece Sarah might have taken it when we cleared out the house. Sarah lives out in Oregon now. It rains so much out there, I don't know how she stands it. She says it's good for her ferns, but I'd miss the sunshine...

Oh, my goodness, listen to me! I'm sorry, doctor, I've completely lost the thread again. What were we talking about? Worrying? No, no, I don't really worry about things like that. Just busy hands, that's all!
Would you say that the feeling of restlessness is always there, even when you're not actively doing something or thinking about a specific task?

Well, I wouldn't say it's *always* there, no. But I do get it when I'm supposed to just sit and listen. Like, when I'm at the senior center meetings, or sitting through the announcements at church. I get this awful ants-in-my-chair feeling, you know? I just have to shift around, or stand up to go get a cup of coffee, or even just straighten up the papers in my lap just to get through it. 

The coffee at the senior center, though, oh my, it is just dreadful. They buy it in those giant plastic tubs, the cheapest brand they can find. And they leave it sitting on those little heating pads for hours until it tastes like burnt rubber! I told Margaret—she's the one who organizes the Tuesday morning bingo—I said, "Margaret, we really ought to chip in and buy some decent beans. Maybe a nice Colombian roast." But she's so tight with the center's budget, you'd think she was paying for it out of her own pocket! Margaret used to work as an accountant for the city, so I suppose it's just ingrained in her. She's got this little ledger book she carries everywhere, recording every penny. It's got a red vinyl cover that's peeling at the corners. My father used to have a ledger just like it for his hardware store. He sold the most wonderful tools. Hammers with real hickory handles, none of this plastic nonsense they have today. The smell of that store was just... sawdust and machine oil and brass polish. I used to sweep the floors for him on Saturday mornings for a nickel...

Oh, dear me! I'm so sorry, doctor. I've done it again, haven't I? Just wandering off down memory lane. What was the question? Oh, the restlessness! Yes, just when I have to sit still for too long, like at the meetings. That's when I get that antsy feeling!
Would you say that this restlessness has been happening on most days and that it significantly affects how you go about your day?

Well, I suppose it does happen most days, yes. It certainly gets in the way of things. Like at the senior center, I've had to apologize after meetings because I just can't seem to settle down. And one of my friends—that's Betty, she's a dear, but very particular—she actually suggested I take a smaller role at the sign-up table because my manner was making things tense. 

Betty has always been like that, though. Very proper. She used to be a librarian over at the main branch downtown. You know, the one with those big stone lions out front? They always reminded me of the lions at the New York Public Library, though of course ours aren't nearly as grand. I went to New York once, in the fall of 1971. We saw a Broadway show—Fiddler on the Roof, I think it was. Oh, the music was just spectacular. We stayed at this little hotel near Times Square, and the noise! Sirens and honking all night long. My husband, God rest his soul, he brought earplugs, but I couldn't stand having things in my ears. I still can't. Even those little headphones the young people wear nowadays, they just look so uncomfortable. My grandson has a pair that are bright green, and he walks around the house nodding his head to music I can't even hear...

Oh, for heaven's sake, listen to me rattle on! I am so sorry, doctor. I keep doing that. But yes, to answer you, it does happen most days, and it does make things a bit difficult, like at the sign-up table.
Do you ever feel like your mind keeps going over the same thoughts again and again, even if you don't want it to, like something you can't quite control?

No, I wouldn't say that. My mind doesn't really get stuck like a broken record or anything. It's more like... well, it just bounces from one thing to the next, like a pinball! But I don't sit there dwelling on the same thought over and over. 

Now, my neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he is just like that. He will get an idea in his head and he just cannot let it go. Last month, it was the elm tree in my front yard. He was absolutely convinced the roots were going to crack his driveway. He came over three times a week to talk about it! I finally had to have the arborist out—a very nice young man named David, who actually went to high school with my grandson. David said the roots were perfectly fine and growing the other way. He showed me on this little electronic tablet he carried. It's amazing what they can do with those things now. My daughter bought me one for Christmas two years ago so we could do those video calls. It has a lovely pink case that folds up into a little stand. But I can never remember which button turns the camera on, so half the time she's just looking at my ceiling! I have this beautiful textured wallpaper on the ceiling in the living room, you know. We put it up in 1982 to cover some water stains after the big blizzard. Oh, the snow that year was just incredible. It was piled higher than the mailboxes...

Oh, my stars! There I go again! I am so sorry, doctor. I just can't seem to stay on track today. What were you asking me? Oh, about thoughts getting stuck? No, no, they don't get stuck. They just like to travel a bit too much!
Have you noticed that your restlessness is something other people can see, like fidgeting, pacing, or an inability to sit still for more than a few moments?

Well, I suppose they must be able to see it. Like I mentioned, Betty certainly noticed when I was at the sign-up table, and I do get those ants in my pants at the meetings. I'm always shifting my weight or fixing my skirt. 

I buy most of my skirts at that lovely little boutique on Main Street—Eleanor's, it's called. Eleanor herself is retired now, but her daughter runs it. She has such wonderful taste, though the prices have certainly gone up since the eighties. I remember buying a beautiful wool blend skirt there for just twenty-five dollars! It was a lovely forest green, perfect for autumn. Autumn is my favorite season, you know. The leaves turning those brilliant oranges and reds. We used to drive up to Vermont every October just to see the foliage. My husband would pack a picnic basket with those little cucumber sandwiches he liked so much. He always cut the crusts off, said they ruined the texture. I never minded the crusts myself. In fact, when I make toast in the mornings, I like it a bit well-done, almost burnt. I use that wonderful sourdough bread from the bakery next to the pharmacy. The baker there, an Italian fellow named Giuseppe, he always gives me a little extra loaf if I come in right before closing. He says it's because I remind him of his grandmother in Naples. I've never been to Italy, though I always wanted to go. I imagine the pasta there is just divine...

Oh, good heavens, I've done it again, haven't I? I am so terribly sorry, doctor! My mind just takes a little walk and forgets to come back! What did you ask? Oh, if people can see me being restless. Yes, I'm quite sure they can, what with all my fidgeting and adjusting.
Would you say that your restlessness often shows up as fidgeting with your hands, tapping your feet, or moving around more than others might expect in the same situation?

Well, let's see... fidgeting with my hands or tapping my feet? I don't really think I do that, no. I mean, I shift around in my chair, like I said, but I'm not sitting there drumming my fingers or tapping my toes like a tap dancer. 

Though speaking of tap dancing, my grand-niece Sarah takes tap lessons. She's just seven, and she had her very first recital last month. She wore this adorable little blue sequined outfit. Her mother—that's my niece, Susan—made the costume herself. Susan has always been so clever with a sewing machine. She made her own wedding dress, you know. It had this beautiful lace overlay that she found at an antique shop in Boston. We took the train up there just to look for fabric. I love taking the train. It's so much more relaxing than flying. You just sit back and watch the scenery go by. We went past this one farm that had a whole herd of those fluffy cows—Highland cattle, I think they're called. They look like they have bangs! I always wondered if they can see properly with all that hair in their eyes. Like that sheepdog my neighbor used to have, Barnaby. He was always running into the porch steps...

Oh, my goodness, I am so sorry, doctor. There I go again, wandering off into the weeds! What were we talking about? Tapping my feet? No, I don't think I really do that sort of thing.
Would you say that even when there's nothing specific to do, you still feel like you need to be moving or doing something, just to feel right?

Yes, actually, that's exactly it. In fact, that's really what brings me in to see you. For the past year or so, I just feel like I'm always puttering around, fixing things, arranging this and that, or volunteering for just one more thing. Even at 87 years old, I just have a terribly hard time sitting down and being still! 

Like with the volunteering—I just signed up to organize the baked goods for the church bazaar next month. I always bake my lemon pound cake for it. It's my mother's recipe, you know. She got it from a lovely woman she met on a cruise to Alaska back in 1958. They went on one of those magnificent old ocean liners. They really don't make ships like that anymore, all real mahogany wood paneling and brass fixtures. The crew had to polish that brass every single morning. I always wondered what kind of polish they used to keep it so shiny with all that salt air. Salt air is just terrible for metal, you know. When my late husband and I had a little summer cottage near Cape Cod, the hinges on the screen door would rust completely solid every three years. We’d have to go down to the local hardware store—Mr. Abernathy ran it—to buy new ones. Mr. Abernathy was such a sweet man. He always kept a big glass jar of those little soft peppermint candies on the counter. The kind that just melt right in your mouth...

Oh, my heavens! Look at me, off on another journey! I am so sorry, doctor. I was talking about peppermints and hardware stores, wasn't I? What was your question again? Oh, about needing to keep busy! Yes, yes, that's it exactly. I just can't seem to sit and relax. I always have to be puttering!
Would you say that this restlessness happens in most places, like at home, in meetings, or even when you're out running errands, or does it mostly happen in certain places or situations?

Well, I suppose it's just about everywhere, really. It doesn't matter if I'm at home trying to watch Jeopardy, or down at the grocer's, or at my church committee meetings. I just always have that feeling. 

Speaking of the grocer's, I was at the Piggly Wiggly just yesterday—they still have one a few towns over, can you believe it? I always go there for their produce because the supermarket in town just leaves their tomatoes sitting in the cold cases, and a cold tomato is completely ruined, texturally speaking. My grandmother taught me that. She grew the most enormous beefsteak tomatoes in her backyard. She lived in this charming little yellow house with a wrap-around porch. We used to sit out there on the porch swing in the evenings and listen to the cicadas. The porch swing was painted this lovely robin's egg blue, but the paint was always chipping off. My grandfather meant to repaint it, but he was always so busy with his woodworking. He made the most intricate birdhouses. He built one that looked exactly like a miniature Victorian mansion, with little shingles and everything. A family of wrens moved into it the very first spring. Wrens are such busy little birds, always darting about...

Oh, for heaven's sake, I've done it again! I am so sorry, doctor. I was talking about wrens, of all things! My mind is just like a butterfly today, flitting from one flower to the next. What did you ask me? Oh, about where I feel restless. Yes, it's pretty much everywhere I go, I'm afraid.
Would you say the feeling inside is more like a quiet need to be doing something, or more like a tense, uncomfortable urge to move or act?

Well, it's definitely more of a tense, uncomfortable urge. Like when I'm at the senior center meetings, or sitting through the church announcements, I get this terrible ants-in-my-chair feeling. 

Speaking of church announcements, Reverend Thomas really does drag them out lately. Last Sunday he spent ten minutes just talking about the upcoming spring potluck. I'm bringing my deviled eggs, of course. The secret is a little pinch of dry mustard and just a tiny splash of sweet pickle juice. My older sister Eleanor taught me that. She used to make them for all the family picnics out at Miller's Pond. Oh, Miller's Pond used to be so beautiful in the summertime. We’d rent these little green wooden rowboats. One time, my cousin Arthur dropped one of the oars right into the water, and we just spun in circles for nearly an hour! We laughed so hard we cried. Arthur was always getting into funny little scrapes like that. He actually ended up joining the Navy, which we all thought was hilarious considering he couldn't even manage a simple rowboat. He was stationed in Hawaii for a while in the sixties. He sent me a postcard with a hula dancer on it that I kept on my refrigerator for years and years. I always wanted to visit Hawaii, but the flight is just so terribly long...

Oh, my stars! Look at me, sailing clear across the Pacific Ocean! I am so sorry, doctor. I don't know why my brain insists on taking the scenic route today. What were you asking me? Oh, right, about what the feeling is like. Yes, it's very uncomfortable. I get those ants in my chair, and I just have to shift around, or stand up to go get a cup of coffee, or even just straighten the papers in front of me just to get through the meeting.

Would you say your restlessness is primarily about needing to be active and busy, or does it also involve a sense of inner anxiety or worry that something might go wrong if things aren’t done a certain way?

Well, I wouldn't say it's worry, exactly. I don't sit there thinking something terrible will happen if I don't fold the napkins right that second. It's just that I need to be doing *something*. 

Although, speaking of napkins, I was just looking at my linen closet the other day. I have this beautiful set of damask napkins that belonged to my mother-in-law. They have a delicate little embroidered 'H' in the corner. She was very particular about her linens, always had them starched stiff as a board. She used to hire a lady named Mrs. Higgins to come in and do the ironing every Tuesday. Mrs. Higgins was a lovely woman, but she had the most peculiar habit of humming the same tune over and over while she ironed. It was always "Oh, Susannah." My husband—he was just a little boy then—used to hide behind the parlor door and try to whistle along with her. He was terrible at whistling, though. He’d just sort of blow air out of his lips and make a funny little squeaking sound. We had a parakeet once that made a sound just like that. We named him Petey. Petey was a very smart bird. He learned how to unlatch his cage door and would fly right into the kitchen when I was trying to cook...

Oh, dear me! There I go again, off to the races! I am so sorry, doctor. I was talking about Petey the parakeet, wasn't I? What was the question? Oh, about worrying! No, no, it's not worry. It's just that I simply must keep busy, or I feel like I'm going to jump right out of my skin.

inference_history.note: Initial presentation of persistent activity without rest, possible anxiety, OCD, or other behavioral disturbance; no significant ruling out yet.

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose they must be able to see it. Like I mentioned, Betty certainly noticed when I was at the sign-up table, and I do get those ants in my pants at the meetings. I'm always shifting my weight or fixing my skirt. 

I buy most of my skirts at that lovely little boutique on Main Street—Eleanor's, it's called. Eleanor herself is retired now, but her daughter runs it. She has such wonderful taste, though the prices have certainly gone up since the eighties. I remember buying a beautiful wool blend skirt there for just twenty-five dollars! It was a lovely forest green, perfect for autumn. Autumn is my favorite season, you know. The leaves turning those brilliant oranges and reds. We used to drive up to Vermont every October just to see the foliage. My husband would pack a picnic basket with those little cucumber sandwiches he liked so much. He always cut the crusts off, said they ruined the texture. I never minded the crusts myself. In fact, when I make toast in the mornings, I like it a bit well-done, almost burnt. I use that wonderful sourdough bread from the bakery next to the pharmacy. The baker there, an Italian fellow named Giuseppe, he always gives me a little extra loaf if I come in right before closing. He says it's because I remind him of his grandmother in Naples. I've never been to Italy, though I always wanted to go. I imagine the pasta there is just divine...

Oh, good heavens, I've done it again, haven't I? I am so terribly sorry, doctor! My mind just takes a little walk and forgets to come back! What did you ask? Oh, if people can see me being restless. Yes, I'm quite sure they can, what with all my fidgeting and adjusting.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's restlessness is linked to a hyperactive component, such as excessive fidgeting or observable overactivity, which could support a diagnosis of ADHD or differentiate from generalized anxiety.

patient.answer:
Well, let's see... fidgeting with my hands or tapping my feet? I don't really think I do that, no. I mean, I shift around in my chair, like I said, but I'm not sitting there drumming my fingers or tapping my toes like a tap dancer. 

Though speaking of tap dancing, my grand-niece Sarah takes tap lessons. She's just seven, and she had her very first recital last month. She wore this adorable little blue sequined outfit. Her mother—that's my niece, Susan—made the costume herself. Susan has always been so clever with a sewing machine. She made her own wedding dress, you know. It had this beautiful lace overlay that she found at an antique shop in Boston. We took the train up there just to look for fabric. I love taking the train. It's so much more relaxing than flying. You just sit back and watch the scenery go by. We went past this one farm that had a whole herd of those fluffy cows—Highland cattle, I think they're called. They look like they have bangs! I always wondered if they can see properly with all that hair in their eyes. Like that sheepdog my neighbor used to have, Barnaby. He was always running into the porch steps...

Oh, my goodness, I am so sorry, doctor. There I go again, wandering off into the weeds! What were we talking about? Tapping my feet? No, I don't think I really do that sort of thing.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences inner restlessness or a subjective need to move, even when not actively engaged in tasks, which would be more indicative of a primary restlessness or hyperactivity rather than anxiety-related symptoms.

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that for the past year or so I feel like I’m always puttering, fixing, arranging, or volunteering for one more thing, and even at 87 I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the constant need to be moving or doing something, which corresponds to the symptom of being 'on the go' or acting as if 'driven by a motor'.

patient.answer:
Yes, actually, that's exactly it. In fact, that's really what brings me in to see you. For the past year or so, I just feel like I'm always puttering around, fixing things, arranging this and that, or volunteering for just one more thing. Even at 87 years old, I just have a terribly hard time sitting down and being still! 

Like with the volunteering—I just signed up to organize the baked goods for the church bazaar next month. I always bake my lemon pound cake for it. It's my mother's recipe, you know. She got it from a lovely woman she met on a cruise to Alaska back in 1958. They went on one of those magnificent old ocean liners. They really don't make ships like that anymore, all real mahogany wood paneling and brass fixtures. The crew had to polish that brass every single morning. I always wondered what kind of polish they used to keep it so shiny with all that salt air. Salt air is just terrible for metal, you know. When my late husband and I had a little summer cottage near Cape Cod, the hinges on the screen door would rust completely solid every three years. We’d have to go down to the local hardware store—Mr. Abernathy ran it—to buy new ones. Mr. Abernathy was such a sweet man. He always kept a big glass jar of those little soft peppermint candies on the counter. The kind that just melt right in your mouth...

Oh, my heavens! Look at me, off on another journey! I am so sorry, doctor. I was talking about peppermints and hardware stores, wasn't I? What was your question again? Oh, about needing to keep busy! Yes, yes, that's it exactly. I just can't seem to sit and relax. I always have to be puttering!

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose it's just about everywhere, really. It doesn't matter if I'm at home trying to watch Jeopardy, or down at the grocer's, or at my church committee meetings. I just always have that feeling. 

Speaking of the grocer's, I was at the Piggly Wiggly just yesterday—they still have one a few towns over, can you believe it? I always go there for their produce because the supermarket in town just leaves their tomatoes sitting in the cold cases, and a cold tomato is completely ruined, texturally speaking. My grandmother taught me that. She grew the most enormous beefsteak tomatoes in her backyard. She lived in this charming little yellow house with a wrap-around porch. We used to sit out there on the porch swing in the evenings and listen to the cicadas. The porch swing was painted this lovely robin's egg blue, but the paint was always chipping off. My grandfather meant to repaint it, but he was always so busy with his woodworking. He made the most intricate birdhouses. He built one that looked exactly like a miniature Victorian mansion, with little shingles and everything. A family of wrens moved into it the very first spring. Wrens are such busy little birds, always darting about...

Oh, for heaven's sake, I've done it again! I am so sorry, doctor. I was talking about wrens, of all things! My mind is just like a butterfly today, flitting from one flower to the next. What did you ask me? Oh, about where I feel restless. Yes, it's pretty much everywhere I go, I'm afraid.

doctor.question: Would you say the feeling inside is more like a quiet need to be doing something, or more like a tense, uncomfortable urge to move or act?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: When I'm at the senior center meetings or sitting through church announcements, I get this ants-in-my-chair feeling and have to shift around, stand up for coffee, or straighten papers just to get through it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the subjective, internal feeling of restlessness (whether it's a tense, uncomfortable urge to move), which corresponds to the adult manifestation of feeling restless.

patient.answer:
Well, it's definitely more of a tense, uncomfortable urge. Like when I'm at the senior center meetings, or sitting through the church announcements, I get this terrible ants-in-my-chair feeling. 

Speaking of church announcements, Reverend Thomas really does drag them out lately. Last Sunday he spent ten minutes just talking about the upcoming spring potluck. I'm bringing my deviled eggs, of course. The secret is a little pinch of dry mustard and just a tiny splash of sweet pickle juice. My older sister Eleanor taught me that. She used to make them for all the family picnics out at Miller's Pond. Oh, Miller's Pond used to be so beautiful in the summertime. We’d rent these little green wooden rowboats. One time, my cousin Arthur dropped one of the oars right into the water, and we just spun in circles for nearly an hour! We laughed so hard we cried. Arthur was always getting into funny little scrapes like that. He actually ended up joining the Navy, which we all thought was hilarious considering he couldn't even manage a simple rowboat. He was stationed in Hawaii for a while in the sixties. He sent me a postcard with a hula dancer on it that I kept on my refrigerator for years and years. I always wanted to visit Hawaii, but the flight is just so terribly long...

Oh, my stars! Look at me, sailing clear across the Pacific Ocean! I am so sorry, doctor. I don't know why my brain insists on taking the scenic route today. What were you asking me? Oh, right, about what the feeling is like. Yes, it's very uncomfortable. I get those ants in my chair, and I just have to shift around, or stand up to go get a cup of coffee, or even just straighten the papers in front of me just to get through the meeting.

patient.answer:
Well, I wouldn't say it's worry, exactly. I don't sit there thinking something terrible will happen if I don't fold the napkins right that second. It's just that I need to be doing *something*. 

Although, speaking of napkins, I was just looking at my linen closet the other day. I have this beautiful set of damask napkins that belonged to my mother-in-law. They have a delicate little embroidered 'H' in the corner. She was very particular about her linens, always had them starched stiff as a board. She used to hire a lady named Mrs. Higgins to come in and do the ironing every Tuesday. Mrs. Higgins was a lovely woman, but she had the most peculiar habit of humming the same tune over and over while she ironed. It was always "Oh, Susannah." My husband—he was just a little boy then—used to hide behind the parlor door and try to whistle along with her. He was terrible at whistling, though. He’d just sort of blow air out of his lips and make a funny little squeaking sound. We had a parakeet once that made a sound just like that. We named him Petey. Petey was a very smart bird. He learned how to unlatch his cage door and would fly right into the kitchen when I was trying to cook...

Oh, dear me! There I go again, off to the races! I am so sorry, doctor. I was talking about Petey the parakeet, wasn't I? What was the question? Oh, about worrying! No, no, it's not worry. It's just that I simply must keep busy, or I feel like I'm going to jump right out of my skin.
